A2.text:
Farid and his sister Gunel love Korean series. Every Friday evening in Baku, they make tea and binge-watch three episodes together. They do not understand Korean, so they always read the subtitles.

Last week, they watched a detective show. The plot was very exciting, and the cast was great. An old policeman, Detective Park, was not the main actor, but he was wonderful. “He can steal the show in every scene,” Gunel said. Even the soundtrack made them nervous: it was the kind of music that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

At midnight, they started the last episode. Suddenly, the internet stopped. The screen went black right on a big cliffhanger: Detective Park was opening a secret door.

“No!” Farid shouted. “Who is behind the door?”

The next morning at university, Farid's friends talked about the series. Farid put his hands over his ears. “No spoiler, please!” he said.

In the evening, the internet still did not work. Gunel had an idea. “Let's write our own ending,” she said. “Come on, give it a shot!”

They wrote three different endings and laughed all night. On Sunday, they finally watched the real ending — and they liked their own sequel much better.

B1.text:
Every Friday night in their flat near Ganjlik, Farid and his sister Gunel turn off their phones, make a big pot of tea and binge-watch whatever series they have chosen for the month. This autumn it was a Korean detective show. Neither of them speaks a word of Korean, so they watched it with English subtitles.

From the first episode, the plot kept them guessing. The whole cast was strong, but an elderly side character — a tired policeman called Detective Park — managed to steal the show every time he walked into a room. Even the quiet piano soundtrack made ordinary scenes feel dangerous; it was the sort of story that keeps you on the edge of your seat for hours.

At midnight they clicked on the finale. Detective Park was standing in front of a locked basement door, key in hand — a classic cliffhanger. And then the storm outside cut the neighbourhood's internet.

All Saturday, Farid moved through university like a man walking through a minefield. Everyone in the cafeteria was talking about the finale, and twice he had to cover his ears and shout, “Please, no spoiler!”

By Saturday evening the connection was still dead. Farid stared at the blank television in despair, until Gunel dropped a notebook and two pens on the table. “We know all the clues,” she said. “Let's write Episode Twelve ourselves. Come on, give it a shot.”

They argued for three hours, drank two pots of tea and ended up writing not only the ending, but the outline of a whole sequel. When the internet finally came back on Sunday morning and they watched the real finale, they looked at each other in silence.

“Ours was better,” Farid said.

“Much better,” Gunel agreed.

B2.text:
Farid and his sister Gunel had turned Friday nights into a small ritual: phones face down, a pot of thyme tea on the table, and three episodes in a row of whatever series they had decided to binge-watch that month. In October it was a Korean thriller set in a foggy port town. Neither of them knew more than three words of Korean, so they relied entirely on the English subtitles.

What made the show remarkable wasn't the central mystery — the plot had a few holes if you thought about it too hard — but the cast. In particular, there was a retired inspector named Detective Park, a minor character with a crumpled raincoat and a habit of feeding stray cats, who managed to steal the show every time the camera found him. Add a haunting cello soundtrack, and even a scene of two people waiting for a lift had Farid and Gunel on the edge of their seat.

They reached the final episode at midnight. Detective Park was standing before a locked door at the docks, the music rising toward a classic cliffhanger — and then a gust of Baku wind brought down a line in the courtyard and took the router with it.

Saturday at university was an obstacle course. Half of Farid's faculty seemed to have watched the finale, and he spent his breaks dodging conversations so nobody could drop a spoiler.

By eight that evening the internet was still dead. Gunel watched her brother pacing the carpet, then slid a blank legal pad across the table. “We've watched eleven hours of clues,” she said. “Why don't we write the last twenty minutes ourselves? Come on — give it a shot.”

What began as a joke turned into four hours of fierce negotiation over motives, alibis and what Detective Park would actually say. By the time they went to sleep, they had not only finished the series but sketched out an entire sequel.

The internet returned at dawn. They watched the official finale over breakfast, waiting for the brilliance they had been promised. When the credits rolled, Gunel quietly closed the laptop.

“They got Detective Park completely wrong,” she said.

Farid nodded, already reaching for the legal pad.

options: Two siblings who discover that imagining an ending together is more rewarding than the show itself
A technical failure that ruins a brother and sister's relationship
Why foreign thrillers lose their meaning in translation
A university student who writes scripts for television
questions.why: Forced to invent the finale themselves, they find their version understands the characters better than the real one.

questions.why: Disappointed by the official ending, they prefer their own version and the sequel they sketched out.

podcast.title: Just one more episode

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: What was the last series you watched? Guess: who in this episode stayed up until 4 a.m. watching a series — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is films and series. And Leyla looks very tired.
[sigh] Because I only slept three hours. Last night I started a new series at ten o'clock...
And?
And I finished the whole first season at four in the morning. I wanted to binge-watch two episodes, not eight!
[laugh] What happened?
Every episode ended with a cliffhanger. The hero is falling from a building — and then, black screen. How can you sleep after that?
You can't. That's the trick. They keep you on the edge of your seat.
Exactly. The plot was so clever. And the soundtrack! I'm still singing the music.
So tell me — how does it end?
No! No spoilers. You have to watch it yourself.
Thank you. I hate spoilers. My brother once told me the ending of a film in the cinema queue.
That's terrible! [laugh] Is the cast good, at least, in the things you watch?
In my favourite film, yes. The main actor is great, but sometimes a small character can steal the show. In this one it's an old taxi driver. He's so funny.
I love that. And do you watch sequels? I'm always disappointed.
Usually the first film is better. But not always.
Okay, here's a tip for English learners: watch with English subtitles, not Azerbaijani or Turkish ones.
Yes! You hear the words and see them at the same time. It's like a free English lesson.
And choose something you really like. Then it doesn't feel like studying.
If you're not sure, try a comedy series. The episodes are short. Give it a shot.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what film or series would you recommend — without spoilers?
And Leyla — sleep tonight, please. See you next time!
[laugh] One more episode... Bye for now!
